title: VII. Ilusha
paragraphs: The doctor came back out of the room, wrapped in his fur coat, cap on his head. His face looked almost angry and disgusted, as though he were afraid of getting dirty. He threw a cursory glance around the passage, looking sternly at Alyosha and Kolya as he did. Alyosha waved to the coachman from the door, and the carriage that had brought the doctor drove up. The captain darted out after the doctor and, bowing apologetically, stopped him to get one last word in. The poor man looked utterly crushed, a scared look in his eyes.

"Your Excellency, your Excellency ... is it really possible?" he began, but couldn't go on, and clasped his hands in despair. Still, he gazed at the doctor imploringly, as though a single word from him might yet change the poor boy's fate.
"I can't help it, I'm not God!" the doctor answered offhandedly, though with his usual air of importance.
"Doctor ... your Excellency ... and will it be soon, soon?"
"You must be prepared for anything," the doctor said, in sharp, emphatic tones, and, dropping his eyes, made to step out toward the carriage.
"Your Excellency, for Christ's sake!" the terrified captain stopped him again. "Your Excellency! But can nothing, absolutely nothing, save him now?"

"It's out of my hands now," the doctor said impatiently, "but h'm!..." he stopped suddenly. "If you could, for instance ... send ... your patient ... at once, without delay" (he spoke the words "at once, without delay" with an almost wrathful sternness that made the captain jump) "to Syracuse, the change to the new, be-ne-ficial climate might possibly bring about—"
"To Syracuse!" the captain cried, unable to grasp what he'd heard.
"Syracuse is in Sicily," Kolya suddenly cut in, by way of explanation. The doctor looked at him.
"Sicily! your Excellency," the captain faltered, "but you've seen" — he spread his hands, gesturing at his surroundings — "mamma and my family?"

"N—no, Sicily isn't the place for the family — the family should go to the Caucasus in early spring ... your daughter must go to the Caucasus, and your wife ... after a course of the waters in the Caucasus for her rheumatism ... must be sent straight to Paris, to the mental specialist Lepelletier — I could give you a note for him, and then ... there might be a change—"
"Doctor, doctor! But look!" The captain flung his hands wide again, in despair, indicating the bare wooden walls of the passage.
"Well, that's not my department," the doctor grinned. "I've only given you the answer medical science has to your question about possible treatment. As for the rest, to my regret—"

"Don't worry, apothecary, my dog won't bite you," Kolya rapped out loudly, noticing the doctor's rather uneasy glance at Perezvon, standing in the doorway. There was a note of anger in Kolya's voice. He used the word "apothecary" instead of "doctor" on purpose, and, as he explained afterward, used it "to insult him."
"What's that?" The doctor jerked his head up, staring at Kolya in surprise. "Who's this?" he asked Alyosha, as if expecting an explanation.
"It's Perezvon's master, don't worry about me," Kolya said, incisively again.
"Perezvon?" the doctor repeated, baffled.
"He hears the bell, but can't say where it is. Goodbye, we'll meet again in Syracuse."
"Who is this? Who is this?" the doctor flew into a towering rage.

"He's a schoolboy, doctor, a mischievous boy — pay him no mind," Alyosha said, frowning and speaking quickly. "Kolya, hold your tongue!" he cried at Krassotkin. "Pay him no mind, doctor," he repeated, somewhat impatiently.
"He wants a thrashing, a good thrashing!" the doctor stamped his foot in a fury.
"And you know, apothecary, my Perezvon might just bite!" Kolya said, turning pale, his voice trembling, his eyes flashing. "_Ici_, Perezvon!"
"Kolya, one more word out of you and I'll have nothing more to do with you," Alyosha cried, peremptory.
"There's only one man in the world who can give orders to Nikolay Krassotkin — this is the man," Kolya said, pointing to Alyosha. "I obey him — goodbye!"

He stepped forward, opened the door, and hurried into the inner room. Perezvon flew after him. The doctor stood frozen for five seconds in amazement, staring at Alyosha; then, cursing, he hurried out to the carriage, repeating aloud, "This is ... this is ... I don't know what this is!" The captain dashed forward to help him into the carriage. Alyosha followed Kolya back into the room. He was already at Ilusha's bedside. The sick boy was holding his hand and calling for his father. A minute later the captain came back too.

"Father, father, come ... we ..." Ilusha stammered, in violent excitement, but, unable to go on, he flung his wasted arms around his father and Kolya both, drawing them together into one embrace, hugging them as tightly as he could. The captain suddenly began shaking with silent sobs, and Kolya's lips and chin twitched.
"Father, father! How sorry I am for you!" Ilusha moaned bitterly.
"Ilusha ... darling ... the doctor said ... you'll be all right ... we'll be happy ... the doctor ..." the captain began.
"Ah, father! I know what the new doctor said to you about me.... I saw!" Ilusha cried, and again hugged them both with all his strength, hiding his face against his father's shoulder.
"Father, don't cry, and when I die, get a good boy, another one ... choose one of them all, a good one, call him Ilusha, and love him instead of me...."
"Hush, old man, you'll get well," Krassotkin suddenly cried out, in a voice that sounded angry.

"But never forget me, father," Ilusha went on, "come to my grave ... and, father, bury me by our big stone, where we used to go for walks, and come to me there in the evening, with Krassotkin ... and Perezvon.... I'll be expecting you.... Father, father!"
His voice broke. All three of them fell silent, still embracing. Nina was crying quietly in her chair, and at last, seeing everyone in tears, "mamma" too burst into tears.
"Ilusha! Ilusha!" she exclaimed.
Krassotkin suddenly freed himself from Ilusha's embrace.

"Goodbye, old man, mother's expecting me back for dinner," he said quickly. "What a shame I didn't tell her beforehand! She'll be dreadfully worried.... But after dinner I'll come back to you for the whole day, the whole evening, and I'll tell you all sorts of things, all sorts of things. And I'll bring Perezvon — but I'll take him with me now, because he'll start howling without me and bother you. Goodbye!"
And he ran out into the passage. He didn't want to cry, but out in the passage he burst into tears anyway. Alyosha found him crying.
"Kolya, you must keep your word and come, or he'll be terribly disappointed," Alyosha said firmly.
"I will! Oh, how I curse myself for not coming sooner!" Kolya muttered, crying, no longer ashamed of it.
At that moment the captain flew out of the room and at once shut the door behind him. His face looked frantic, his lips trembling. He stood before the two of them and flung up his arms.

"I don't want a good boy! I don't want another boy!" he muttered in a wild whisper, clenching his teeth. "If I forget thee, Jerusalem, may my tongue—" He broke off with a sob and sank to his knees before the wooden bench. Pressing his fists against his head, he began sobbing with absurd, whimpering cries, doing everything he could to keep the sound from reaching the room.
Kolya ran out into the street.
"Goodbye, Karamazov! Will you come yourself?" he called out sharply, almost angrily, to Alyosha.
"I will, certainly, this evening."
"What was that he said about Jerusalem?... What did he mean by that?"
"It's from the Bible. 'If I forget thee, Jerusalem' — that is, if I forget everything most precious to me, if I let anything take its place, then may—"
"I understand, that's enough! Mind you come! _Ici_, Perezvon!" he cried, with real ferocity, at the dog, and strode off home with rapid steps.
